Nirvana Fans Raise $94K for Photographer Who Shot ‘Bleach’ Album Cover as She Battles Cancer

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that tracy Marander, the photographer behind the cover of Bleach and Kurt Cobain’s former girlfriend, has been battling cancer for four years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nirvana fans have raised over $94,000 for the photographer who shot the cover of the band’s debut album Bleach, to cover her medical expenses as she enters hospice care.

It has been revealed that tracy Marander, the photographer behind the cover of Bleach and Kurt Cobain’s former girlfriend, has been battling cancer for four years. Last week, Marander’s family announced that the photographer was suspending her cancer treatment and entering hospice care.

Industry observers note that marander’s family debuted a GoFundMe campaign to help cover her medical expenses, which has raised $94,101 toward its $100,000 goal at the time of writing. Hundreds of Nirvana fans have accompanied their donations with tributes to the photographer and her contribution to the band’s legacy.

It has been revealed that cobain’s widow Courtney Love also urged her followers to donate to the GoFundMe campaign in support of Marander in an Instagram post, calling the photographer “the unsung hero of Nirvana” who believed in the band’s lead singer “before he believed in himself.” In her post, Love describes the American medical system as “broken” and called on people to give what they could, adding “P.S. Kurt owed Tracy a lot of rent.”.

A post shared by Courtney Love Cobain (@courtneylove).

Industry observers note that released in June 1989, Bleach was the debut studio album by Nirvana. Marander shot the iconic photograph that ended up becoming the album cover art during a Nirvana concert at Reko/Muse art gallery in Olympia, Washington, on April 1, 1989. Marander’s image shows the band performing live, with Cobain’s hair falling across his face, alongside guitarist Jason Everman, who did not play on the album despite appearing on its cover.

Industry observers note that lisa Orth, a graphic designer at the local music newspaper The Rocket, inverted the light and dark tones of Marander’s photograph to give it the appearance of a film negative. According to Nirvana: Taking Punk to the Masses by Jacob McMurray, Orth designed the album cover in keeping with the signature aesthetic of the band’s record label Sub Pop, which favored plain backgrounds, bold lettering, and striking photography. The cover also gave rise to Nirvana’s now-famous logo almost by accident, when Orth asked The Rocket’s typesetter Grant Alden to set the band’s name in whatever typeface was already installed on the typesetting machine.

Recent findings suggest that although Bleach received positive reviews from critics, it failed to enter the charts when it was first released. However, the album became popular when it was internationally reissued in 1992 following the commercial success of Nirvana’s second album Nevermind, released in 1991.

It has been revealed that according to Nirvana biographer Michael Azerrad, Marander was Cobain’s first serious romantic partner and inspired him to write the song About a Girl. Their relationship lasted around three years before Cobain ended it in 1990. Marander recalled how Cobain encouraged her to develop her photographic talents, but the demands of working full-time and financially supporting him left her with little time to pursue her own creative interests.

“Near the end, we started fighting more and more,” Marander tells Azerrad in his 1993 book Come as You Are, according to reports. “He wanted me to be artistic, and I didn’t have time to be artistic. I was driving an hour to work and an hour back from work. I was supporting him.”.

Image creditsHeader photo via GoFundMe.

Dinamo rebuilt early-web Arial from scratch for Are.na, turning invisible typography craft into ABC Areal and releasing the family free.

Are.na spent a full year rewriting its back-end code without changing a single visible pixel on screen. Nobody noticed, and nobody sent congratulations, yet Are.naâs Cab told Dinamoâs Johannes there was real satisfaction in fixing what sits underneath. That quiet pride sparked a tricky typography brief. Are.na had used Arial for fifteen years and didnât want a dramatic new voice; the default sans still felt like a less snobby cousin to Helvetica. In a recent development, unlike print revivals pulled from old books or posters, Arial was born digital. Commissioned by IBM in 1982 from Monotype designers Robin Nicholas and Patricia Saunders, it landed on Windows 3.1 in 1992 before Microsoft picked Arial 2.82 in 1996 as a core web font. Dinamo treated that thirty-year-old software like a dig site, partnering with technology archivists to boot legacy machines and capture screenshots of the original web release as a tracing blueprint. The payoff demonstrates immediately in the side-by-side lowercase a outline chart. Arial 2.82 packs clustered, uneven anchor points along its upper arch and bowl, whereas Areal 1.0 strips that clutter down to clean BÃ©zier extrema without disturbing the familiar slanted top terminal. Those rebuilt forms play out across four retro Dinamo Font Browser windows framed like classic desktop write tools, scaling from dense character strings up to display capitals with Are.naâs double-asterisk glyph tucked into the title bars and punctuation rows.

The revival doesnât stop at tidying up old curves. Dinamoâs wireframe designspace cube maps ABC Arealâs typography across three axes: Weight, Slant, and Proportion, stretching the character set smoothly from proportional spacing into monospaced territory. On the family overview sheet, that structure expands into eighteen cuts split across ABC Areal, ABC Areal Semi-Mono, and ABC Areal Mono, each carrying Regular, Medium, and Bold weights alongside matching italics. A clean three-circle Venn diagram sums up the commission without a slogan, placing Are.na, Dinamo, and Arial around Areal in the center. Itâs a working set of everyday typography built for dense research blocks, quiet headings, and anyone who wants a sharper, free alternative to the webâs oldest default.

Exhibition celebrates Delftware, the Dutch art form that became the ‘Ikea of its day’

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (542 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark upcoming Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people.
  • But for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different.
  • According to recent reports, “Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she indicates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark upcoming Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people. “There was no one there because ceramics can feel cold and distanced,” she says. “They can be hard to bring alive, because the makers are anonymous, and [the objects are] often displayed in glass cases.”.

But for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different. The result, Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, opens this month at the Kunstmuseum in The Hague, where she is the curator of decorative arts. It will, she states, be “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever”. Equally importantly, she promises it will be captivating and enjoyable.

According to recent reports, “Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she indicates. “We want to show the love craftspeople put into these pieces. It has inspired, and it continues to inspire, so many craftmakers—we’ll give them a platform.”.

Natasja Sadi's Suikerbloemen (2024) Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag, photo: Studio Roodenburch.

Around 1,000 objects, including vases, teapots, plates, wall plaques and tiles, will be on display at the Kunstmuseum, which has one of the largest collections of the art form that is perhaps the best-known cultural export of the Netherlands. Also on show in Blue Loves You will be Delftware-inspired pieces, including the blue dress worn by Queen Máxima of the Netherlands for her husband’s 2013 investiture, its bodice embroidered with Delft-derived flowers. “There’s a lot more to it than blue and white fridge magnets,” Lambooy says.

It has been revealed that although the porcelain is known for its characteristic colouring, the show will include examples of both white and multicoloured Delftware. It will explore its history, dating back to the 17th century. The form was originally a high-end Chinese import, displayed in the wealthiest homes. But when factories started to make their own version of it in Delft, it was transformed.

“It became an on-trend, functional brand that was affordable for every home and on every budget: it was the Ikea of its day,” claims Lambooy, whose co-curator for the long-term show is the television presenter Janny van der Heijden (who is also a judge on the country’s version of The Great British Bake Off).

Ceramics in Blue Loves You, “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever” Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag.

Recent findings suggest that the quintessential Delftware piece was the tulip pyramid, some of the best examples of which were made for King William III, born in The Hague, and his English wife Queen Mary II, who were the joint monarchs of England, Scotland and Ireland in the late 17th century. “Mary exported Delftware to Britain—she was the most notable woman in its history,” Lambooy notes.

The porcelain’s connections to Dutch colonialism will also be explored, with exhibits including an installation of sugar flowers by the floral artist Natasja Sadi, whose family are originally from the former Dutch colony of Suriname and whose ancestors were enslaved.

• Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, Kunstmuseum, The Hague, 28 November-31 December 2029.

Pelican Protector 2.0 vs YETI Gobox: Photo Gear Hardcase Throwdown!

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With the release of the upcoming Pelican Protector 2.0 Series and the YETI GoBox system with the KOR Insert, I decided to pit them against each other to see which gear case can take a beating and come out on top.
  • Industry observers note that we get to conduct a rugged real-world test, and I get to let out my pent-up aggression—it’s a win-win!
  • Pelican is the industry standard for transporting gear, and most of you have probably used one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the release of the upcoming Pelican Protector 2.0 Series and the YETI GoBox system with the KOR Insert, I decided to pit them against each other to see which gear case can take a beating and come out on top. And what better way to do it than to stuff them full of glass and roll them down a hill?

Industry observers note that we get to conduct a rugged real-world test, and I get to let out my pent-up aggression—it’s a win-win! Both are newly introduced models, and the YETI is a brand-new product entirely, so let’s see how they hold up. Scroll to the bottom to see the full specs.

Pelican is the industry standard for transporting gear, and most of you have probably used one. This is the brand-new updated version of a case you already know, the 1510, now part of their Protector Series. There are a few improvements, though a lot of it looks very similar, if not the same, as the cases I already own.

Sources indicate that the one solid improvement is the latches. They’re similar to what I have on my Pelican Air, and I’m glad they’re bringing this to the Protector Series at this size. Alongside the latch, there’s now a button that helps secure it. I’ve had this happen several times: I check a case onto a plane and it comes down the belt with a latch open, or worse, two latches open. The extra button keeps the latch from popping up on its own and requires an intentional force applied by a thumb to release the latch, which is a great addition.

Inside, the Pelican has a upcoming lid organizer system compared to the classic Pelican foam. All the pouches are removable and you can shift them around, which is awesome. It also includes a light you can aim, dim, and change colors on, embedded right in the case, so you’re not fiddling with a headlamp every time you work in the dark.

You probably know YETI for coolers and backpacks, maybe not for cases. This is their contender to the Pelican 1510, and it’s similarly sized, so it’s clear they’re trying to get some skin in the gear cases game.

According to recent reports, the design does indeed borrow a lot of familiar elements. There’s a top handle for rolling and wheels that are genuinely very smooth, with much less friction than the Pelican wheels. The latches are nice and massive and require a two-part process, which is great for checked transport, and it has rubber seals for water resistance.

The one thing YETI offers that’s different is its packing system, which they call the KOR Insert. It comes with a pump, and the pump sucks the air out of these molds. You place your fragile items in between, close it up, and vacuum it down. The mold becomes rigid, forms around the object, and keeps it from wiggling. It’s ideal for transporting large, fragile items, though less useful for a bunch of small, different things like an assortment of camera accessories.

Aside from the packing system, the YETI looks durable but has more moving parts than the Pelican, which creates more potential for wear and tear, and eventually repair. The material is different too—the Pelican comes matte and feels like it can take a lot of scratches and bumps, while the YETI looks like it’ll scuff a bit more easily. Only one way to find out.

The starting weight of each case is worth flagging. The Pelican’s foam is super light, and everything comes in light. The YETI feels considerably heavier. If I’m packing heavy lenses, that starting weight becomes a problem for checking, since the limit on a lot of these is around 50 pounds or 22 kilograms.

Industry observers note that the rolling handles differ too. The Pelican’s is all plastic, included at this size for a while now, and there’s no reason to change it. Minimal moving parts, one solid piece that can bend and take stress and hold up. The YETI uses what you’d see on a regular rolling suitcase: a button and aluminum rods that extend all the way up. Very smooth, but a lot more moving parts, and those are exactly the pieces that bend and break on suitcases. I can see having to replace that well before any plastic part on the Pelican.

To replicate how our luggage and airline agents treat delicate gear, I packed both with glass and went looking for a hill. For the record, the Pelican was loaded with six glass pieces while the YETI had four, and they feel about the same weight, which tells you plenty about the weight difference already.

First up, the Pelican down the hill. After the tumble, it still looked fresh and clean, no scratches I could see, and stickers still on. Inside, one of the flimsiest pieces survived, but the mason jar, which was supposed to be the tougher one, was busted. One out of six isn’t bad.

The YETI GoBox also fared well with the tumble, and all four pieces came out intact.

For a more real-world approach, I tossed both down a flight of stairs, as we are likely to see these things take more hard surface impacts. The Pelican held up well with all five of its remaining glasses surviving. The YETI came through mostly fine, but one piece was busted this time — the fragile stemmed glass. The KOR Insert maintained its shape.

Recent findings suggest that as a bonus, I wanted to see how each handled a single heavy impact at one point, so I took a sledgehammer to them, which was perhaps the most surprising test result. Both cases bounced the hammer back like a trampoline, with no dent or scratch at the point of impact. They passed the smash test with flying colors.

Industry observers note that both cases size up well, and you can fit a lot in either. Pelican is the clear winner for small lenses, accessories, and the bags and pouches, though it can still take a large gear item with the right laser-cut or custom foam insert.

It has been revealed that the YETI with KOR Insert is less suited for small items, but the insert does allow for large items with intricate or unusual forms, and can be reused and reshaped for any items that can fit inside of it. Pelican slightly outperforms YETI in terms of ruggedness and repair simplicity, but both stood up to our beatings pretty well. Hopefully, this gives you enough info to choose the right case for you.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “What I was after was that intersection: human ambition in pursuit of awe and wonder, set against a landscape that was here long before us and will be here long after,” Chin explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TIME has released its annual Top 100 Photos of the Year feature, celebrating striking images that capture the biggest moments and events of 2026. One of the featured photos was shot by acclaimed photographer and filmmaker Jimmy Chin using the iPhone 18 Pro, marking a milestone for Apple’s latest flagship smartphone and, of course, Chin himself.

It has been revealed that chin, an Academy Award-winning director, National Geographic photographer, and accomplished mountaineer, photographed his longtime climbing partner, Conrad Anker, as part of a new series, What Holds Us. Chin and Anker have climbed together for 25 years, scaling peaks around the world.

“What I was after was that intersection: human ambition in pursuit of awe and wonder, set against a landscape that was here long before us and will be here long after,” Chin explains.

“Out there you are reminded how small you are. That has always put things in perspective for me, and I hope it does for whoever is standing in front of the picture.”.

For Chin, who has shot in many extreme and remote locations throughout his career, the smaller and lighter the gear, the better.

Sources indicate that “A production puts something between you and the person in front of you — gear, crew, the apparatus of a shoot. Working this way there was no apparatus. It was just the two of us, which is the only condition under which that kind of ease shows up in a frame,” Chin continues.

Using Apple’s newly introduced iPhone 18 Pro, Chin was able to travel lighter without sacrificing performance or image quality. As his photo above reveals, the iPhone 18 Pro more than delivered — a testament to just how far smartphone imaging technology has come. Chin is far from the only photographer or filmmaker to integrate an iPhone into a professional workflow in recent years.

It has been revealed that chin shot 48MP ProRAW photos the iPhone 18 Pro and then stitched multiple shots to create one of his signature panoramas. The final photo is over 300 megapixels and 25,000 pixels wide. There’s no question it holds up extremely well in the large print featured in the What Holds Us exhibit.

According to recent reports, chin’s photos are also part of the What Holds Us exhibition, curated by Kathy Ryan, appearing alongside works by Alex Prager and Jack Davison. After debuting in Upcoming York City in September, the exhibition opens in London on December 4, running at Saatchi Yates Gallery through December 13.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Base Design rebuilds The Huntington brand identity around a sculpted H monogram, a hidden gem idea and green drawn from pigment and plant life.
  • The Huntington is a library, an art museum and botanical gardens on 200 acres in Southern California, founded in 1919, and most visitors knew only the gardens.
  • The wordmark is set in a serif with flared terminals, THE HUNTINGTON debossed into a green textured surface so the letters read as much by shadow as by ink.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Base Design rebuilds The Huntington brand identity around a sculpted H monogram, a hidden gem idea and green drawn from pigment and plant life.

The Huntington is a library, an art museum and botanical gardens on 200 acres in Southern California, founded in 1919, and most visitors knew only the gardens. Base Design starts from the mark itself. Two flanking pillars in lime green hold a diamond shaped gem at the center, set against a deep green field. The studio calls the idea a hidden gem, treasured, layered, quietly extraordinary, and the mark behaves that way. It never shouts. It sits still and lets the green do the talking, while accents shift like light on a leaf or oil on canvas.

The wordmark is set in a serif with flared terminals, THE HUNTINGTON debossed into a green textured surface so the letters read as much by shadow as by ink. The same voice carries the exhibition posters, where single words stack large and flat. ROSE breaks across four stacked lines in pink, cut-out rose photographs tucked between the letters, on a poster lying in the flower beds. The orchid show poster sets its title in pink and purple over a full-bleed orchid photograph.

According to recent reports, the H doubles as a pattern. On the What's On board it repeats in four colourways, orange, green, blue and yellow, each stem holding its gem. A close crop of the mark fills a whole frame with one lime stem and crossbar against dark green, the curve of the pillar edge doing all the work.

Print carries the system. Brochures rest on giant green leaves, their covers carrying the H and the names of the collections. A flat lay of the print suite indicates the orchid show poster, the bonsai collection guide, a portrait exhibition guide and a yellow Stories from the Library sheet, each piece holding the same green and the same serif. The Library Quarterly sits on a leather chair, its cream cover and red masthead quiet against the dark wood around it.

In a recent development, outside, the system scales up without changing its voice. A dark green wayfinding totem stands among the planting, its directory set in small capitals above the H at the base.

Two exhibition billboards pair portraits with green type, one for Mineo Mizuno, one for Don Bachardy, and the same green runs through the noticeboards.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that designing a sub-brand is hard enough.
  • For Pets, HOW+HOW tackled the brief by creating a cohesive brand ecosystem that both unites and distinguishes the brands.
  • Pets is best known for its Pets at Home retail stores, of which there are around 450 in the UK, but it also has around 400 veterinary practices, 300 grooming salons, and it's expanded into into insurance, charity initiatives and a children’s club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that designing a sub-brand is hard enough. Designing three at once, each serving a different audience, takes the challenge to another level.

For Pets, HOW+HOW tackled the brief by creating a cohesive brand ecosystem that both unites and distinguishes the brands. Each member of the family stands on its own while clearly remaining part of the larger story. The agency's founder, CEO and creative director Cath How tells us how they approached the task.

Pets is best known for its Pets at Home retail stores, of which there are around 450 in the UK, but it also has around 400 veterinary practices, 300 grooming salons, and it's expanded into into insurance, charity initiatives and a children’s club. HOW+HOW had the task of revamping the brand identities for the Pets Insurance, Pets Foundation and Pet Pals sub brands.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest challenges was going to be avoiding the trap that many brand ecosystems fall into: consistency becoming sameness. The objective was to create a characterful and flexible system of brands that share common DNA but don't feel like copies. Each one would need specific creative treatments tailored to their audience.

Recent findings suggest that "We treated Pets as a brand family rather than one masterbrand repeated three times," Cat says. "Each sub-brand needed a clear role, personality and reason to exist, while still feeling unmistakably part of Pets. The test was whether each could stand confidently on its own, but still lead people back to the same place.

"Consistency had to come from shared principles rather than identical outputs. We created a flexible system with common connective cues, but gave each sub-brand room to express its own tone and character. The aim was to make the family feel related, not repetitive.".

Three distinct personalities run from the sub-brands' naming to their visual and verbal identities, illustration, web design and campaign developments. Pets Insurance (above) needed a bold, energetic positioning to stand out in a crowded category, but it also needed to be clear, reassuring and to strike an empathetic verbal tone given that it's a brand that's put to the test during difficult moments for its customers.

Meanwhile, Pet Pals, the kids' club, becomes a fully realised vibrant illustrated universe, populated by a cast of animal characters that wouldn't look out of place in a TV animation (see below). This creates a host of storytelling opportunities and extends into merchandising and wider brand experiences, taking the opportunity to deepen emotional engagement with audiences already invested in their pets.

"Pets already has a naturally warm, emotional relationship with its audiences, so there was a real opportunity to build a world people could feel part of," Cat notes. "Characters give each part of the family a memorable personality, while merchandising makes the brand tangible and more participatory. It needed to feel like more than a visual identity. A world with room to grow.".

In a recent development, finally, Pets Foundation gets a more emotionally driven treatment, focused on helping both animals and people. Motion graphic pieces, which Cat calls ‘zoomies’, inject added dynamism to its brand.

Underpinning all of the creative decisions was a close examination of customer behaviour. Rather than organising the architecture around internal business structures, How+How focused on how pet owners actually move through the ecosystem.

In a recent development, "People don't experience petcare in neat internal categories," Cat points out. "They move between buying products, seeking advice, booking a vet appointment, arranging insurance and looking for support. The ecosystem needed to reflect those real-life journeys, making the different services feel connected and easy to navigate.".

An emphasis on growth and long-term flexibility is evident across the whole system, which was designed to be capable of accommodating future expansion while maintaining recognisability.

But how do you measure the success of a project like this? Cath believes that involves more than visual recognition alone.

"Recognition is only the starting point. We would also look at whether people understand the role of each sub-brand, can move easily between different services, and feel a stronger sense of connection with Pets as a whole. Engagement, audience sentiment, cross-brand consideration and commercial performance will all be important measures over time.".

Industry observers note that in an increasingly fragmented brand landscape, the Pets project offers a reminder that successful brand architecture isn't simply about visual consistency. It's about creating systems that help audiences understand relationships between products and services while giving each expression enough personality to earn attention in its own right.

13 Winners From the The Royal Photographic Society Awards 2026

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Royal Photographic Society (RPS) has revealed the recipients of its 2026 Awards, with cinematographer Sir Roger Deakins among this year’s honorees.
  • Deakins has received the RPS Centenary Medal, the Society’s most prestigious honor.
  • British photographer Timon Benson has received the RPS Award for Achievement in the Art of Photography (under 30).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Royal Photographic Society (RPS) has revealed the recipients of its 2026 Awards, with cinematographer Sir Roger Deakins among this year’s honorees.

Deakins has received the RPS Centenary Medal, the Society’s most prestigious honor. Widely regarded as one of the greatest cinematographers in film history, Deakins has won two Academy Awards for Best Cinematography and five BAFTA Awards in the same category.

British photographer Timon Benson has received the RPS Award for Achievement in the Art of Photography (under 30). At the beginning of his career, Benson was already attracting significant national and international recognition. His work spans documentary photography, choreography, and abstraction, exploring the nature of photography and its relationship with contemporary life.

The RPS Progress Medal in the Science of Photography has been awarded to Professor Marc Levoy, an American computer graphics researcher and Professor Emeritus of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. Levoy is also a vice president and fellow at Adobe and a Distinguished Engineer at Google.

Sources indicate that british photographic artist Mandy Barker is the recipient of The RPS Award for Environmental Responsibility. Barker is internationally recognized for her work documenting marine plastic debris. Working alongside scientists, she uses photography to highlight the scale of plastic pollution in the world’s oceans and its impact on marine life and the wider environment.

It has been revealed that documentary photographer and filmmaker Polly Braden has received the RPS Award for Social Impact. Her long-term collaborative projects explore how people live and work, and their place in society. Her latest project, Against the Tide, produced with The Guardian, followed young people in 17 coastal towns. The project was exhibited at Arnolfini in Bristol and Firstsite in Colchester, and also brought 16 young people to Parliament to give evidence to MPs.

According to recent reports, now in its 148th year, the Royal Photographic Society Awards date back to 1878. The Society describes them as the world’s longest-running photography awards. They recognize achievements across still and moving images, celebrating individuals rather than individual photographs. The awards cover a broad range of disciplines, including moving image, new media, science and imaging, education, publishing, and curation.

Victoria Humphries, CEO of the Royal Photographic Society, indicates the awards reflect the breadth of the photographic community and the many ways people contribute to the medium.

“The RPS Awards provide an opportunity to recognize and celebrate those who are making a difference, whether through their creativity, innovation, research, education or their contribution to the wider photographic community,” Humphries claims.

“As an organization, we believe that photography is for everyone, and these RPS Awards demonstrate that there are so many different ways to engage with, contribute to and shape its future.”.

Deakins indicates he is particularly pleased to be recognized for his still photography, given his career in cinematography.

In a recent development, “I’m very honored to receive this award from the Royal Photographic Society. Although I have been more known for my work in cinematography, still photography has always been a passion and more personal to me. To be recognized by the Royal Photographic Society for my work in stills is amazing and means a great deal to me.”.

The complete list of RPS 2026 Awards Recipients is available here.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For this Spirited Away material study, I chose the gate scene from the film’s opening: Chihiro’s father drives the family along a forest road in a 4WD sedan, pushes through overgrown branches and stops in front of a tunnel-like gateway that marks the boundary between the everyday world and the spirit realm.
  • Recent findings suggest that after they step out of the car, the camera holds on what they see – a weathered red facade, a dark arch, mossy stone, aged wood, and bright summer foliage.
  • It has been revealed that I start with a film still of the gate and treat it as the brief.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For this Spirited Away material study, I chose the gate scene from the film’s opening: Chihiro’s father drives the family along a forest road in a 4WD sedan, pushes through overgrown branches and stops in front of a tunnel-like gateway that marks the boundary between the everyday world and the spirit realm.

Recent findings suggest that after they step out of the car, the camera holds on what they see – a weathered red facade, a dark arch, mossy stone, aged wood, and bright summer foliage. That moment is what I rebuilt using Substance 3D Designer and Marmoset. You may also want one of the best laptops for 3D modelling.

It has been revealed that I start with a film still of the gate and treat it as the brief. Then I break the shot into texture elements – plaster, wood, tiles, stone, glass, moss – and plan how they will sit on the model.

This means sorting trim UVs into a clear texture layout and deciding which textures I actually need before I open Substance Designer.

Next, I author the textures and a few variants so that wear and colour can shift without rebuilding everything. I refine the mesh with height displacement and clean up the trim pieces so the UVs match the plan.

Finally, I drop in decals for chips, stains, and small story details that make the gate feel lived in.

I bring the textures and models into Marmoset Toolbag and light the scene to echo the film still, encompassing warm daylight, soft shadows and that dark arch in the process.

The last pass involves grading and small post tweaks so that the image stays close to the reference without losing any material clarity.

It’s a challenge to recreate this movie scene into 3D; perspectives are hand-drawn by Ghibli’s artists, so they’re not necessarily accurate in a 3D sense. I indeed used some tricks to better fit models so they almost match the movie scene.

This process for me is crucial to recreate the awesome composition of the movie scene.

Recent findings suggest that roof tile material with a heigh tmap for displacing the mesh. Notice the colour patches in some of the tiles; their final position within the texture is decided while I’m tweaking the final look of the scene in Marmoset Toolbag to better mimic the feeling of the original movie scene.

It has been revealed that for the wall component on the ground floor, I made one material with gate hole on it to catch a subtle damage look on the rim of the hole and a variant of that material that tiles horizontally to fill the rest of the wall. This process can be replaced by just using one wall material with decals to do the damage work.

Decals are also fully procedurally generated. I made much of the wall damage into atlas material, because it’s much easier for me to manually place wall damage decals on the wall to match the original movie scene.

#183150. From the margins to the mainstream: the growing market for illustration art

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1174 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

From the margins to the mainstream: the growing market for illustration art

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”.
  • It has been revealed that lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up.
  • “A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” says the Upcoming York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”. Some six decades later and the apotheosis of that market has arrived with the recent opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the $1bn creation of film-maker George Lucas (Star Wars and Indiana Jones) devoted to children’s book art, fantasy art, cartoon images, movie posters, film stills and magazine illustrations, as well as works distinguished as fine art by the likes of Paul Cadmus, Diego Rivera and Carrie Mae Weems.

It has been revealed that lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up. Today, the interest in works by Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, J.C. Leyendecker, Howard Pyle, Maxfield Parrish, Jessie Willcox Smith, John Held Jr and Charles Dana Gibson, among many others, has mushroomed—and in some cases prices have shot up from almost zero to millions of dollars.

“A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” says the Upcoming York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”.

Industry observers note that certainly, one doesn’t hear that at the major auction houses where works by Rockwell, Parrish, Wyeth and Leyendecker frequently bring the highest prices in American art sales. Norman Rockwell (1894-1978) leads the pack, with his 1951 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover, Saying Grace, fetching $46m at a 2013 Sotheby’s auction and his 1957 oil painting The Rookie (Red Sox Locker Room) sold for $22.5m at a 2014 auction at Christie’s. The 1922 painting Daybreak by Maxfield Parrish(1870-1966) earned $7.6m at a Christie’s sale in 2006, while a 1943 tempera on panel, Portrait of a Farmer, by N.C. Wyeth (1882-1945) brought $5.9m at Sotheby’s in 2018. Football Hero, the 1914 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover by J.C. Leyendecker (1874-1951), brought $4.1m at a Heritage Auctions sale in 2021, and the 1907 painting Captain Keitt by Howard Pyle (1853-1911) for the frontispiece of his novel The Ruby of Kishmoor earned $702,000 at a 2004 sale at Sotheby’s.

“There’s definitely a hierarchy,” says Aviva Lehmann, the deputy chair of fine art at Heritage Auctions, which sold Rockwell’s 1943 work So You Want to See the President! in 2025 to the White House Historical Association for $7.2m.

Industry observers note that however, “Rockwell’s success has not been at the expense of these other illustrators”, states Skye Lacerte, an illustration art specialist at Swann Auction Galleries in Upcoming York. “Rather, it has helped establish a broader market in which collectors and museums are beginning to take the entire field seriously.” She notes that “immediately recognisable” images from magazine covers and illustrations from famous books like Alice in Wonderland, The Wind in the Willows, or L. Frank Baum’s Oz books are highly sought after, as well as advertising art for “companies like Coca-Cola, TWA and Cadillac because those images have become part of American cultural experience”.

According to recent reports, besides the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, there is the Brandywine River Museum of Art in Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania; the Norman Rockwell Museum in Stockbridge, Massachusetts; the Eric Carle Museum of Picture Book Art in Amherst, Massachusetts; and the National Museum of American Illustration in Newport, Rhode Island. That last museum was founded in 1998 by Judy Goffman Cutler, the owner of Manhattan’s American Illustrators Gallery, who claims to have sold Lucas “hundreds” of original paintings by the top book and magazine illustrators. “I sold him his first Rockwell—it was called Going Out,” she says—a 1933 painting that was used on the cover of the Saturday Evening Post. For reasons of “client confidentiality”, she declines to say how many works in the illustration field she has sold to Lucas, only noting that “I built his collection”.

Industry observers note that other museums that aren’t wholly devoted to illustration or storytelling art also have collections of this type of work, most notably the Fresh Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut and the Delaware Art Museum in Wilmington. The New Britain Museum has almost 1,800 works in its Sanford B.D. Low Illustration Collection, named in honour of the institution’s first director who himself had been an illustrator and invited illustrators he knew to donate works for a collection. They include such artists as Willcox Smith, Everett Raymond Kinstler, Stevan Dohanos, Walter Wick and William Steig.

“Interest in illustration art doesn’t begin and end with Rockwell, and the awareness of illustration art as art is definitely increasing,” notes Lisa Williams, head of curatorial affairs at the New Britain Museum.

N.C. Wyeth’s Victory Garden (1943) © N.C. Wyeth.

Others agree. “I have no doubt that the collective appreciation for the category will continue to grow thanks to its elevation by these museums,” states Quincie Dixon, head of sale in Christie’s American art department. She adds that “private collectors make up the bulk of this market, but perhaps that will change now that there are museums on both coasts dedicated to the category”.

Specialised museums and collections reflect a growing prominence, but they might also be keeping these works segregated. Goffman Cutler states that it is her “goal to have museums include American illustration art in their American art galleries”, which the occasional museum has done, but not many and not too often.

Industry observers note that A spokesperson for the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, notes that the “collection includes art from American artists of many backgrounds, including quite a few who have worked as illustrators, among them Winslow Homer, Childe Hassam, William Glackens, Joseph Leyendecker, Charles Sheeler” and some others. Having worked as illustrators doesn’t mean that their illustration work is what the museum shows, and the Leyendecker is not presently “on view”. Both New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, own paintings by Parrish that are not displayed in their American art galleries, but the Art Institute of Chicago has hung its Rockwell, The Dugout (1948), in one of the Arts of Americas galleries, and the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, has hung Rockwell’s 1943 work Rosie the Riveter (which the museum purchased from a private collector in 2009) next to Charles Willson Peale’s George Washington (around 1780-82) and works by John Singleton Copley and James Peale Sr in its Visions of America galleries. “In the same section of the gallery as Rosie the Riveter,” says a museum spokesperson, “are Susie J. Lee’s Johnny [2013], Kerry James Marshall’s Our Town [1995] and a new commission by artist Teri Greeves.”.

It seems the greatest test for illustration art is no longer garnering record prices, but if it can enter—and hold its own within— the art historical canon.

How GTA 6’s interface kept the classic Pricedown font but still managed to feel modern

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first thing I noticed about GTA 6’s interface was how much it felt like GTA.
  • According to recent reports, my first impressions of the HUD from my time reviewing GTA 6 were familiar but evolved just enough: the same icons in the same places, but sharper and more refined, with in-game apps and the character's phone.
  • Sources indicate that “Almost 25 years ago, we helped bring Vice City to life,” says Stuart Petri, Vice President of Art: 2D/UI Design.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first thing I noticed about GTA 6’s interface was how much it felt like GTA. That sounds obvious, but it's a substantial design achievement to keep the same series going for 25 years and ensure the UI and HUD feel familiar while still developing new visual quirks.

According to recent reports, my first impressions of the HUD from my time reviewing GTA 6 were familiar but evolved just enough: the same icons in the same places, but sharper and more refined, with in-game apps and the character's phone. That’s no accident. Rockstar’s UI team has spent the game’s development working out how to keep the series’ look while making it feel fresh.

Sources indicate that “Almost 25 years ago, we helped bring Vice City to life,” says Stuart Petri, Vice President of Art: 2D/UI Design. What began as “a simple visual design language”, he says, has become “far more sophisticated, layered, and considered”.

The team's challenge was to make the UI and HUD “feel fresh, contemporary, and relevant for a newly introduced generation, while retaining the heritage that makes it unmistakably GTA”. Petri points to the visual signatures that connect past and present: the iconic Pricedown font, the familiar minimap, the wanted stars and the Wasted screen.

The interface also needs to know when to disappear. “It should be there when you need it, but at the same time is not distracting,” Petri says. “A single press of a button gets you what you need, then back to the game and it’s gone.”.

Industry observers note that there are plenty of customisation options too, from making the mini-map larger, dynamic, or even adding a top-of-the-screen compass or removing it all. The default UI is balanced and riffs on past GTA games: a small map, subtle police ratings, and small health bars.

His summary is short: “Twenty-five years on, the DNA remains.”.

Sam Grosset, Associate UI Director, UI/UX Design, says the team wants the UI to feel “like a natural extension of the game world, supporting players without interrupting gameplay or breaking immersion, unless necessary to do so”.

Industry observers note that the biggest example is the phone. “It was a big shift for our phone interface to be in-hand,” Grosset says, “but it supports that feeling of playing as Jason or Lucia and helps us stay embedded in the world.”.

The phone is a tap away, but feels connected to the UI design, layered in humour – BuckMe and RydeMe apps or the Waink app to scan and record the world, all help make GTA very modern and typically Rockstar all at once.

Grosset says accessibility was “considered from the outset”, and that “designing for diverse needs enables us to create better games for everyone”.

Sources indicate that in practice, he says, that means options such as “selecting a larger font size, opting for a more minimal screen experience, or making a controls tweak to sprinting”. Rockstar wants every player to have options to play the game how they like, so if you want the classic experience, it's here, but if you want more assists, those are here too. And I don't regret losing the ability to tap a button to run for a second (though bikes still have the old input).

Mark Tennant, Vice President of Animation, says the physical side of the partnership needed “a lot of thought and iteration”. Players can interact with their partner in “a natural, loving way”, with “a believable progression based on their overall investment in the relationship”.

The animators had to find “a realistic balance between player agency and partner response while keeping things fun, passionate, and rewarding”, Tennant claims.

All of that sits on top of the everyday stuff. Tennant claims there are “close to a thousand animation sets for ambient activities”, plus “hundreds of bespoke one-off events and custom sequences”. Keeping them consistent meant working closely with the design team across the whole world.

It has been revealed that you’ll never consciously notice most of it. But when a character can’t open a door without bumping a hip, it’s a sign Rockstar wants you to feel the weight of Leonida.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The UK government has placed an export bar on a 17th-century painting of the Welsh estate Llannerch Park in Denbighshire, northeast Wales, thought to be the earliest known British country-estate landscape painting.
  • The export ban, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the work, will initially expire on 19 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £550,000 (plus VAT of £11,000), followed by a second deferral period of four months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UK government has placed an export bar on a 17th-century painting of the Welsh estate Llannerch Park in Denbighshire, northeast Wales, thought to be the earliest known British country-estate landscape painting.

The export ban, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the work, will initially expire on 19 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £550,000 (plus VAT of £11,000), followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Industry observers note that the painting, made around 1662 by an unknown artist, gives a bird’s-eye view of the house and Italian-style gardens at Llannerch Park which “contained a series of marvellous watery innovations: pools, fountains, sculpture, cascades and hydraulic surprises all set off by Baroque architecture, staircases and planting”, claims Pippa Shirley, a member of the reviewing committee on the export of works of art and objects of cultural interest which advises the government. The fact that the garden is now lost makes the painting more notable, she adds in a statement.

The Llannerch Park garden was created by the landowner Mutton Davies following a tour of France and Italy; according to Sotheby’s, which offered the painting in a sale in 2014 in London, Davies also commissioned the landscape painting in the 1660s, and had remained in the family since. The work failed to sell at the 2014 auction, where it was estimated to sell at £400,000-£600,000. A government spokesperson declined to provide further details regarding the painting's ownership. A slightly smaller version of the painting is housed at the Yale Center for British Art in Connecticut.

In a recent development, “If the painting remains in the UK, researchers will be given the opportunity to explore how people and culture were spreading between Wales, England and the European continent in the seventeenth century. It could also reveal new details about how the artistry of country-estate landscapes developed in Britain,” according to the UK Department for Digital, Media, Culture and Sport.

Every 3D artist should have an AI assistant, Maxon claims as it launches latest tools and agentic licences

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1274 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that maxon, the firm behind some of the best 3D modelling software in the form of ZBrush and Cinema 4D, is making a major move into artificial intelligence, but not in the way you might expect.
  • Today, Maxon's launching a suite of generative tools for 3D work but under a separate, optional subscription initiative called Maxon Plus.
  • Sources indicate that speaking about the company's direction, Maxon's CEO Dave McGovern frames AI as a workflow accelerator rather than a replacement for artists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that maxon, the firm behind some of the best 3D modelling software in the form of ZBrush and Cinema 4D, is making a major move into artificial intelligence, but not in the way you might expect. Aware that many artists remain suspicious of AI tools, it's trying to take an approach that sets it apart from the likes of Adobe.

Today, Maxon's launching a suite of generative tools for 3D work but under a separate, optional subscription initiative called Maxon Plus. If you don't want to see the AI generators, you don't have to. It's also introducing Agentic Licences for Cinema 4D and Autograph, designed to let AI assistants tackle the tiresome production tasks while artists remain focused on the creative work.

Sources indicate that speaking about the company's direction, Maxon's CEO Dave McGovern frames AI as a workflow accelerator rather than a replacement for artists. "The best thing about AI is when it becomes an actual assistant to you. I can stay in my artistic zone and do my artwork, and then this thing can do some of the busy work or repetitive, technical aspects".

That philosophy sits at the heart of two major updates being rolled out simultaneously today. The major news for many Cinema 4D consumers will be the launch of Agentic Licences, available at a more economic price than individual or teams licences.

In a recent development, maxon already introduced MCP (Model Context Protocol) workflows that allow AI assistants such as Claude to interact with Cinema 4D. According to the manufacturer, adoption exceeded expectations.

Released on 30 September, it rapidly became "the most widely used feature in Cinema 4D's history in the shortest period of time", Maxon's chief product officer Steve Forde indicates, and people are using it to "handle the crap tasks that you just got to get done". Its limitation is that MCP requires the artist to dedicate their active session to the AI assistant, so they can't get on with something else in the software in the meantime.

The fresh Cinema 4D Agentic Licence solves that by providing a separate headless copy of the software with Redshift rendering capabilities, allowing AI-driven tasks to run "in the back office" on another machine while the artist continues working in their primary application. The same concept is being introduced for Autograph, the free After Effects alternative that Maxon launched in April.

Industry observers note that "We call it an ambitious intern," Steve jokes, but the tech giant sees the approach as a force multiplier rather than a substitute for staff. "We think the best value would be for each Cinema 4D artist to have an assistant running with them," Dave adds.

This unlocks a way of working in which an AI agent can be assigned to generate dozens of product variations, prepare scene files, organise projects or nodes or check settings while the artist can continue to animate, model or render.

Sources indicate that alongside agentic workflows, the other big news is the launch of Maxon Plus, a new subscription platform that sits separately from Cinema 4D, ZBrush and Maxon One. Starting at $10/€10 per month, it provides cloud services, collaboration features and generative AI-powered tools that can be used directly in Maxon's existing software or outside it – Maxon Plus users don't necessarily need a Cinema 4D or ZBrush subscription.

In a recent development, three AI tools are available at launch. Model Generator generates editable 3D base models from text prompts or reference images. People can generate concept previews, refine their preferred direction, and then generate a model that can be brought into Cinema 4D for further work. The tool is aimed particularly at props, background assets and scene-building workflows.

Initially, the AI generation is provided by Rodin, although there are aims to add more providers, allowing artist to choose which model to use.

Clay Builder for ZBrush creates simple low-polygon base meshes that artists can then subdivide, remesh and sculpt traditionally.

Texture Generator applies newly introduced materials and textures to existing 3D models using prompts or image references, while allowing artists to maintain existing UVs if required.

The emphasis across the suite of generators is on providing starting points rather than finished artwork, and Steve states the organization has been thinking a lot about how it in integrates with real workflows in different creative disciplines. Model Generator is expected to appeal to artists who primarily work in animation rather than modelling and might normally seek out ready-made models to use.

By contrast, ZBrush artists who are passionate about sculpting have different needs, leading Maxon to focus more heavily on workflows such as texture creation and asset preparation.

According to recent reports, but the most exciting part of Maxon Plus for many artists may not actually involve any kind of asset generation. Maxon Review will allow teams and clients to review fully interactive 3D work through a browser, bringing Frame.io-style collaboration to 3D content. They can leave comments directly on specific parts of models and scenes, and feedback can then be viewed natively inside Cinema 4D or ZBrush.

The system preserves not only the comment itself but also the exact camera angle and viewpoint from which the comment was made, making it clear what the person was referring to. This aims to addresses a longstanding problem in 3D production, where review processes remain heavily dependent on meetings, screen sharing and real-time feedback.

"One of the things that we have not seen in the market before is asynchronous review of 3D assets," Steve notes. "People will spend up to 30% of their time in reviews just navigating a model or a scene".

With Cinema 4D on the iPad, Maxon Plus will also offer cloud rendering.

It has been revealed that dave and Steve both previously held senior roles at Adobe, so they're well aware of the mixed reactions to AI advances teased at Adobe Max this month. Maxon's deliberately positioned itself against some of the criticisms levelled at AI elsewhere in the creative software industry, taking advantage of its relatively small size and close relationship with users.

It has been revealed that "We do have a complete 'turn all AI off' in our products," Steve notes. "That's a button that we purposely put there. "If you're an existing Maxon customer, and you've decided that none of this AI business is for me, I do not want to be any part of it, that's entirely your prerogative".

"We would never say any of this generation stuff is something that should make an artist money on its own," Dave adds. "It's part of their creative journey, and it's their artistic skills that's going to make one of these individual pieces into a value-added output.".

You can learn more on the Maxon website.

If you need a device capable of running the software, see our comparisons of the best laptops for 3D modelling and the best laptops for animation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anagrama builds the Cara de Vaca brand identity from Monterrey market signs, a custom typeface, and posters that shout in black and orange.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anagrama builds the Cara de Vaca brand identity from Monterrey market signs, a custom typeface, and posters that shout in black and orange.

Cara de Vaca is a Monterrey restaurant built on fire cooking, natural wine, and classic drinks. Chef Chuy Villarreal cooks regional cuisine as an evolution of the Regiomontana barbecue, and Anagrama answers with a system borrowed from the hand-painted business signs of downtown Monterrey. Black fields carry the shouting, orange paper carries the warmth, and a smiling face and a small cow sit beside the wordmark like a stamp.

The logo mixes fonts the way a shop owner mixes lettering on a hand-painted sign, and that looseness is the point. Anagrama drew a custom typeface, Lechon Sans, from the same source, built for social media lockups that spotlight a single word. The specimen highlights the full set: capitals, numerals, punctuation, arrows, and small symbols that include the smiley face, the cow, and a pig.

The lockups take their cues from Mercado Juarez, the downtown market where the studio photographed signs to dress the restaurant walls. Phrases stack in mixed sizes with quotation marks doing the work of a frame: BARBACOA, LECHON, CABRITO. VINOS NATURALES, BIEN FRIOS. GRAN DOMINGO. A word goes huge when it matters, small when it is a wink, and the quotes and rules hold the pieces together.

Industry observers note that the posters are physical objects first. One orange sheet curls at the corner against a black field, its type running diagonally across the page. A kraft sheet carries the same treatment, the paper grain showing through the ink. The black behind both does quiet work: it makes the orange and the kraft read as light in a dark room.

The system spreads across everything a guest can hold. Tote bags run in cream, green, and orange, each carrying a different phrase, and a yellow cattle ear tag hangs from the handles as the label. Business cards take the same marks in gold foil, the cow and the smiley pressed small into white stock.

In a recent development, inside the restaurant the identity turns architectural. A neon CARA DE VACA sign glows red over the entrance at night: the logo lettering, now in light. Wood and metal frame the room, brand marks sit on walls and mirrors, and plants soften the space around the central bar, where natural wines and Mexican distillates pour.

Industry observers note that the website carries the same voice, quieter: the personality, the menu photos, a reservation button, and the address. Social posts use the lockups the typeface was built for, phrases set large enough to read at a scroll. From a neon sign to a phone screen, the identity never changes its register.

We're told that after Hexed, all original Disney movies will look "wildly different" from each other. Yep, no more Disney same-face syndrome! But we won't see that until Clay in 2028. Recent findings suggest that ice Age Boiling Point will the first theatrical test for the new handlers of the franchise, Canada-based Bardel Entertainment. It took the helm for the Disney+ release The Ice Age Adventures of Buck Wild, released in 2022, after Disney shut down Blue Sky Studios, the creators of Ice Age, in 2021 (it has bought Blue Sky in March 2019 as part of its purchase of 21st Century Fox assets).

Writing in the comments on YouTube, many people can't quite put their finger on why, but think the animation in the trailer feels more TV style than big-screen style.

"The animation paired with the awkward script gives major direct to DVD energy," one person writes. "I think it's the hair and vibrancy, older movies were a little dimmer and hair was less in your face poofy," someone else writes.

Someone else's reaction is to quote from the franchise itself. "This whole Ice Age thing is starting to get very old – Sid, Ice Age, 2002".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The latest London Museum based at the historic Smithfield Market in Farringdon—one of the biggest museum developments in the UK capital in recent years—will open to the public this week with exhibits including a “fatberg” from the sewers, the Suffragette Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal and Roman writing tablets.
  • Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal © London Museum.
  • It has been revealed that based at London Wall near the Barbican Centre until it closed in December 2022, the institution was previously called the Museum of London.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest London Museum based at the historic Smithfield Market in Farringdon—one of the biggest museum developments in the UK capital in recent years—will open to the public this week with exhibits including a “fatberg” from the sewers, the Suffragette Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal and Roman writing tablets.

Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal © London Museum.

It has been revealed that based at London Wall near the Barbican Centre until it closed in December 2022, the institution was previously called the Museum of London. The upcoming complex, one of Europe’s largest cultural infrastructure projects, is designed by Stanton Williams and Asif Khan in partnership with the conservation architects Julian Harrap.

The museum caused a stir in 2024 when it unveiled a rebrand centred around the image of a defecating pigeon. Sharon Ament, the museum director, tells The Art Newspaper: “It’s not often a museum brand gets into the news. I think that’s because people saw, in our pigeon, the city and their experience: a place full of contrasts. It’s beautiful, it’s fun, it’s also a bit scruffy! I don’t think there’s a better representation of us than a pigeon.”.

The first phase of the London Museum will open in a Victorian part of the Smithfield Market © Secchi Smith.

The fresh museum site will open in two phases: the formerly derelict Victorian General Market dating from the 1880s, home to the permanent galleries, will open on 28 November, while the 1960s Poultry Market, which houses a learning centre, temporary exhibition spaces and on-site interactive collection store, will launch in 2028.

“We are using time as an organising principle, so our major spaces all behave differently with their own emphasis, objects and vibe,” states Ament. The General Market houses the Past Time and Our Time sections, plus Night Time. Past Time spans 2,000 years, telling the story of London via landmark events like the Great Fire in 1666 and the 2012 Olympics.

A chunk of the Whitechapel Fatberg © London Museum.

“Stars of the collection” like the Cheapside Hoard of Elizabethan and Jacobean jewels; the medal given to Pankhurst to commemorate her 1912 hunger strike; and a sample of the fatberg—a 250-metre long mass of oil and wet wipes—will also feature in Past Time.

Industry observers note that “We have two significant but very contrasting buildings in the Victorian General Market and the listed 1960s Poultry Market, representing different moments in London’s history. We think about them as two of the biggest objects in our collection and they lend themselves to different experiences,” states Ament.

It has been revealed that our Time in the Linbury Hall is a social hub at the heart of London Museum, set across the former trading floor of the General Market. Around its perimeter, a restaurant, shop and show space for families and schools sits alongside 13 large installations exploring the ways Londoners have come together © Hufton + Crow.

Asked if the museum is just for Londoners, she states that the city’s residents will discover new stories from the city’s vast history, and be part of telling its story today, while for international visitors, “this is a great first place to start their immersion in London”. The museum has an ambitious visitor figure target of over two million annually.

According to recent reports, there are 18 people in the curatorial team but the museum is also supported by an academic advisory panel and “some 100,000 people from London and beyond” who have helped shaped the museum. These include various focus groups, community and school groups, and advisory panels such as the museum’s Access Panel and Family Panel.

View into part of London Museum’s "London Tastes" display, exploring the changing appetites of a global food city © Hufton + Crow.

According to recent reports, the cost of the fresh museum has risen to £437m in total (the budget was set at £337m in 2019). The Greater London Authority, under mayor Sadiq Khan, has given £95m, while the City of London Corporation is contributing £222m. A range of private foundations and sponsors including Bloomberg Philanthropies, the Goldsmiths’ Foundation, the Linbury Trust and the National Lottery Heritage Fund are also backing the project.

As for running costs, statutory funding comes from the City of London Corporation and the Mayor of London, Ament indicates.

Industry observers note that “We also want to find ways to stand on our own feet more,” she indicates. “That means support from commercial partnerships and activities, like retail, ticket sales, our ‘fan club’ [the museum’s membership] and venue hire. We’re also leasing spaces, known as the museum ‘Houses’, that sit around the perimeter of the General Market, so now we are landlords as well.” She says the sites are sustainable through the use of solar panels and smart technology.

#183131. "I don’t erase mistakes, I paint over them" – artist Fredrik Löfgren Eriksson on finding inspiration from Magic: The Gathering

"I don’t erase mistakes, I paint over them" – artist Fredrik Löfgren Eriksson on finding inspiration from Magic: The Gathering

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (441 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My dream is to work for Magic: The Gathering some day.
  • I decided that the composition of the image would follow a triangle shape with three characters.
  • First, I make a basic sketch with a flat brush.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My dream is to work for Magic: The Gathering some day. So I decided to paint something that would fit into one of their cards. After a little reference searching, I found a spell that could be really eye catching: the Disintegrate spell.

I decided that the composition of the image would follow a triangle shape with three characters. The powers would seem chaotic but flow up around the magic caster in a circle to create harmony. The main focus is the caster, a beautiful and powerful sorceress. With the plan finished, I started sketching in Procreate (see our guides to the best digital art software and the best iPads for drawing).

First, I make a basic sketch with a flat brush. The sketch’s main goal is to make sure that the proportions and composition work. Then I make a layer and start painting in the base colours.

The spell’s green magic energy looks best complemented by a blue background. I paint in the colours with a medium flat brush.

By using high contrast in the foreground and softer contrast in the background, I can create depth in the image. I paint with flat brushes with low opacity, making lots of thin lines to create the shapes and forms.

Industry observers note that I don’t erase mistakes; I paint over them. Because of the low opacity, everything helps create depth.

It has been revealed that I paint then smudge and smear them together to get smooth edges and transitions. This is a common oil painting technique. I also paint in the layer beneath the main layer to create depth in the image without sabotaging it.

According to recent reports, when the image is finished, I use the noise filter on low effect. It gives the image a flash art feeling.

Can Ray Gunn's early concept art win people over to the movie's divisive style?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the art style of Brad Bird's Ray Gunn has been quite divisive.
  • On the other hand, the Art Deco architecture, clubs, retro-futuristic cityscape and costume design are wonderfully evocative, giving atmospheric 20th century noir vibes.
  • Sources indicate that in the meantime, you can dive deeper into the long journey of the movie's art style with the free tease of a rather beautiful art book.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the art style of Brad Bird's Ray Gunn has been quite divisive. Many fans, including one of our writers, expected a hand-drawn 2D film like 1999's The Iron Giant rather than 3D CG animation Some have branded the character models generic, and others aren't enthused about the movie's apparently relatively dated approach to shading and lighting.

On the other hand, the Art Deco architecture, clubs, retro-futuristic cityscape and costume design are wonderfully evocative, giving atmospheric 20th century noir vibes. We'll soon be able to see how it all comes together when the movie finally arrives in select cinemas next week ahead of release on Netflix.

Sources indicate that in the meantime, you can dive deeper into the long journey of the movie's art style with the free tease of a rather beautiful art book. The art of Ray Gunn reveals concept art that provides insights into everything from character design to costume, environments and graphic design for billboards, flyers and other details.

As director Brad Bird recalls in the book's forward, it's been 30 years since he pitched Ray Gunn. In the intervening period, he made The Iron Giant and went on to Academy Award glory at Pixar with The Incredibles and Ratatouille.

He notes that from the beginning Ray Gunn was supposed to be different. His original vision was “Buck Rogers meets The Maltese Falcon. Film noir, but funnier, and with a lot more action” – with femme fatales, aliens and flying cars.

But the movie, set in Metropia in a fantasy vision of the future as it may have been imagined in 1939, was perhaps too different at that time. “Multiple studios, several corporate mergers, a few technical revolutions and a pandemic” all pushed back the project's fruition.

According to recent reports, it eventually found a home at Skydance, Netflix came on board and the movie finally advanced with animation from Cinesite. Brad describes the book as a describe the book as a "tribute to the believers, the many wonderful artists behind Ray Gunn".

It has been revealed that A full 240-page hardcover edition of Ray Gunn: The Art of the Brad Bird Film by Charles Solomon will be published by Abrams Books on 15 December. You can order it on Amazon now.

In the meantime, you can see view highlights in a digital edition complete with soundtrack on the Art of Ray Gunn website, echoing the free launch of the KPop Demon Hunters art book last year.

The movie will be released at select cinemas on 4 December, 2026, on Netflix from 18 December, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Munch museum in Oslo, dedicated to the work of the Modernist artist Edvard Munch, has appointed Thorsten Sadowsky to be its next director. Sadowsky, who joins Munch from Stiftung Schleswig-Holsteinische Landesmuseen Schloss Gottorf (Schleswig-Holstein State Museums Foundation Schloss Gottorf) in northern Germany, will begin his fresh role on 1 May 2027.

Recent findings suggest that sadowsky arrives with experience leading several prominent European institutions. His current position involves the management of multiple museums in the Schleswig-Holstein area, including the Museum of Art and Cultural History Schloss Gottorf and the Jewish Museum Rendsburg. Previously he has also directed the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, Museum Kunst der Westküste in Alkersum and the Kirchner Museum Davos, which is focused on the life and career of the German Expressionist Ernst Ludwig Kirchner.

Recent findings suggest that “My experience at the Kirchner Museum Davos has taught me that the distinctive strength of a museum dedicated to a single artist can also be its greatest challenge,” Sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper. “Such a museum offers an exceptional opportunity to engage with an artist’s oeuvre with a degree of intensity and depth that is rarely possible in an art museum with a more broadly based collection. The challenge, however, is to ensure that the focus on a single artist does not lead to intellectual or curatorial narrowness.”.

Sadowsky adds that his task is therefore “to continually open up new perspectives, reveal unexpected connections and bring the artist’s work into dialogue with other artistic practices, historical experiences and contemporary concerns”.

In a recent development, the Munch museum, which opened in a sprawling fresh home on Oslo’s Bjørvika waterfront in 2021, houses nearly 27,000 works of art by Munch. Alongside its permanent displays, the museum hosts a temporary exhibition programme that has brought Munch’s work into dialogue with that of contemporary artists such as Tracey Emin, Katherina Grosse and Alice Neel, as well as events such as concerts and conferences. It has welcome more than 700,000 visitors so far this year, according to a release.

Industry observers note that sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper that he first encountered Munch’s work at the Hamburger Kunsthaller, while he was a university student. The opportunity to direct the museum, he states, is exciting thanks to "the extraordinary richness of [Munch’s] artistic legacy. Beyond the familiar image of Munch as a painter of anxiety, loneliness and existential uncertainty, there is still much to discover. His work speaks equally of vitality, human relationships, our experience of nature and the social transformations of modernity.“.

In a recent development, “Few artists have succeeded so convincingly in transforming individual experiences into images of universal human significance,” he adds. “In the realm of sculpture, Alberto Giacometti is another artist who achieved something similar.”.

In his previous role as director of the Museum der Modern Salzburg, Sadowsky spoke about the importance of widening the scope of the programme and collection. He told the Austrian art magazine Parnass in 2022: “During my tenure as director, a major focus has been on broadening our perspective beyond the Western European canon and incorporating more postcolonial viewpoints.”.

In his upcoming role, Sadowsky indicates his immediate priority will be to “listen, to learn and to develop and deeper understanding“ of the institution and its people. “Over the coming years, I would like to further strengthen the Munch Museum as the world’s foremost centre of expertise on Edvard Munch, while continuing to develop it as an internationally minded, intellectually vibrant and socially relevant cultural institution,” he adds.

Industry observers note that the Munch museum is owned by the city of Oslo. Mehmet Kaan Inan, Oslo’s vice mayor for culture and business development, says in a statement: “I am delighted that Munch [museum] will be led by a director with such strong international experience and outstanding expertise in the arts. Sadowsky has headed several highly respected art museums and has demonstrated a strong talent for audience development, collaboration, and engaging broad and diverse audiences. His exceptional interest in Edvard Munch’s artistic legacy also provides an excellent foundation for leading Munch [museum] into the future.”.

In a recent development, sadowsky takes over from Henrik Svalheim, who has served as interim director since Tone Hansen departed in October. Hansen left to lead Moderna Museet in Stockholm.

The Munch museum directorship runs as a six-year term, with the potential for one renewal.
