After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal.
  • At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy.
  • If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

Conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

As the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

Black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

That is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

In a recent development, the data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Research demonstrates that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

In my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

It has been revealed that that matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

The lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

According to recent reports, faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

Sources indicate that black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

Recent findings suggest that it’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).

Swedish retailer IKEA has unveiled its prediction for 2027’s Color of the Year – a dark, reddish-purple shade called Wild Fig.

Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.

The tech giant describes Wild Fig as “a deep, botanical shade with a rich purple tone”, although in certain lights, it looks closer to an earthy oxblood red.

“Full of character and the unexpected, it brings depth and a daring mindset to everyday spaces,” said Abbey Stark, home furnishing direction leader at IKEA US.

Used across furnishings and accessories, it can provide a subtle touch of colour without being overly aggressive, especially paired with warm woods and neutral shades, IKEA US suggests.

But the tech giant equally pictures it being splashed across entire walls and argues it “unexpectedly fits in” with even brighter colours like baby pink and electric blue – IKEA US’s previous colours of the year.

The company’s Style Guide also pulled out a number of other interior design trends to look out for in 2027, including pattern clashing and Japandi minimalism.

Interior designers have already started making liberal use of Wild Fig, as seen in Note Design Studio’s scheme for the Lammhults showroom in Stockholm, where it blankets walls, floors and ceilings in the entrance, as well as an entire kitchen.

Other predictions for 2027’s colour of the year are set to start rolling in any minute, with Pantone’s set to be unveiled at the start of December.

Paint brand Dulux got ahead of the game when it named a muted green called Soulful Sage as its contender in September.

Some interiors industry insiders, including Dezeen columnist Michelle Ogundehin, have argued at least since the end of the pandemic that “it’s time to reconsider the whole colour of the year carnival”, which was originally invented as a marketing stunt for Pantone’s colour-matching system, much like the Michelin Guide was invented to sell more tyres.

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).

Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

📅 31 Aug 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone.
  • Industry observers note that for wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga.
  • The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

Industry observers note that for wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Industry observers note that extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research indicates that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study demonstrated that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

On the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

By training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

Recent findings suggest that as a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

It has been revealed that then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

According to recent reports, wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

According to recent reports, it all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

It has been revealed that no matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”.

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.
  • An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.
  • Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in new directions.”.

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” remarked the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture.

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” stated Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that she saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

“I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she stated. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”.

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually become established among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an notable influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

Sources indicate that after graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” said Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”.

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

According to recent reports, “We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” said Galiotto. “But the key thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

Industry observers note that “Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… travelling the world as much as we can to see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”.

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

Industry observers note that alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its considered eclecticism.

According to recent reports, “We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he said. “I would say it’s something that’s very notable and it gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”.

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”.

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell in size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.

Looking ahead, the architects remarked their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo remarked there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process, which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

“Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”.

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto said if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”.

Industry observers note that “If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

#183013. Industry News: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1727 w)

Industry News: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • It has been revealed that if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

It has been revealed that if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

Industry observers note that “The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Industry observers note that sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, notes Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that the textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Industry observers note that some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

All things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin says. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

Recent findings suggest that regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin indicates.

Because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin notes. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, notes Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

It has been revealed that and it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin claims. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin claims. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

It has been revealed that that’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health complications.

Recent findings suggest that if left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, states Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really swiftly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

In a recent development, over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra says, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

Industry observers note that because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition issues and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar claims. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research reveals that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

It has been revealed that as researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s vital to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Kilian O’Sullivan.

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest fresh-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction company Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design remarked the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

“Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”.

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” stated Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”.

Elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he stated.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”.

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley said the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The latest development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he said.

“We recently declared that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s new Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”.

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) unveiled the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

#183011. Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

📅 31 Aug 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, cutting back on calories but not losing weight?
  • Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight.
  • The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”.

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research demonstrates starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

Industry observers note that what does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:.

Industry observers note that starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

However, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

According to recent reports, most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

So what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

In a recent development, choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

It has been revealed that weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

In a recent development, that mentioned, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

In a recent development, despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

Tech Report: Estudio A-G uses colour to update 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.
  • Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.
  • Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Sources indicate that monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for fresh inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely upcoming, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”.

Completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing newly introduced energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he noted.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”.

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez said, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

In a recent development, the studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its fresh owners live today,” he said.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and newly introduced materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez mentioned, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”.

Industry observers note that he also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

Text Neck Exercises: Simple Moves to Ease Digital Strain

📅 31 Aug 2024 | ⏱️ 2 min read (383 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Greatist

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you’re caught up in doomscrolling or just checking your work emails, chances are you’re spending a lot of time on your phone.
  • So, hold your phone up to eye level and check out these easy tips to get rid of text neck fast!
  • Also known as “tech neck,” text neck is a term coined by a chiropractor to describe the neck pain you might feel after spending too much time looking down at your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re caught up in doomscrolling or just checking your work emails, chances are you’re spending a lot of time on your phone. But all that screen time can lead to a pesky condition called “text neck.” Hunching over your device can leave you with some severe aches and pains.

So, hold your phone up to eye level and check out these easy tips to get rid of text neck fast!

Also known as “tech neck,” text neck is a term coined by a chiropractor to describe the neck pain you might feel after spending too much time looking down at your phone.

Industry observers note that most of us check our phones with our heads tilted forward and down. When you do this for too long, the muscles in your neck get strained. The muscles in the back are overstretched, while the ones in the front are compressed.

If you have text neck, here’s what you might be dealing with:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth.

Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice Latest-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.

Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.

The manufacturer has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.

The Belsize Park location occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block that once formed part of the Ivy Bank residential estate.

Architecture practice Latest-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

At its heart is a large shared kitchen, centred by a chunky tiled breakfast island, followed by a lounge area with intimate groupings of timber-frame chairs and two khaki-coloured sofas, complementing the glossy green fireplace.

Recent findings suggest that just off this space is a cosy snug that’s been painted a warm ochre hue. It’s separated from the lounge by a custom-made curtain that design studio House of Quinn made from earth-toned fabric offcuts.

Holloway Li is behind the design of the interiors. Instead of doing a through-and-through overhaul, the studio instead aimed to develop a “circular economy aesthetic that felt warm, domestic and low-impact”.

“That ambition aligned with Mason & Fifth’s own sustainability agenda and allowed us to explore how historic buildings like this can be retrofitted in imaginative and progressive ways,” remarked the studio’s creative director Alex Holloway.

In each of the guesthouse’s 56 apartments, the bedrooms are furnished with demountable wardrobes in lieu of fitted joinery.

The wardrobes are made up of lightweight timber parts fixed together with metal brackets rather than glue so that, if necessary, they can be unassembled, flat packed, and re-built elsewhere.

Holloway Li worked with Marble Collective to create countertops and splashbacks for the apartment kitchens; all are crafted from limestone that’s been rejected from quarries because of inconsistencies.

The top edge of the splashbacks has been left slightly craggy and unfinished, further celebrating the stone’s natural flaws.

Almost all of the walls throughout the guesthouse have been simply rendered with multi-finish plaster, and any surface imperfections have been left on show.

“In many cases, the most sustainable decision is restraint,” explained Holloway Li’s senior designer Carrie Coningsby.

“Drawing on principles akin to kintsugi and spolia, the approach celebrates intervention rather than concealing it, embedding repair into the visual language of the space,” she added, referencing historic practices focused on reuse and repair instead of replacement.

Mason & Fifth Belsize Park was shortlisted in the sustainable interior category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects in the running included the winning Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo, which is outfitted with materials salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins, and the London Coffee Factory by Steve Jensen Design, which is structured around a reclaimed timber framework.

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth.

Industry News: Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended).
  • But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s notable to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about upcoming plasma as an anti-aging elixir.
  • Industry observers note that plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s notable to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about upcoming plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Industry observers note that plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

According to recent reports, “It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she indicates.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

What that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

It has been revealed that “There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he says. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”.

Industry observers note that about 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

Recent findings suggest that and the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

“So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” indicates Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

Sources indicate that in the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

At first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

Sources indicate that “If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she notes.

Sources indicate that part of the reason for this, indicates Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, states Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be important to find out for whom this works.”.

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

Sources indicate that “I would call this a phase 1 study,” says Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”.

Interiors project of the year, sponsored by Gaggenau, went to Barcelona-based Raul Sanchez’s renovation of an old sailor’s home. Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was awarded emerging interior designer of the year, with Tokyo-based Keiji Ashizawa taking the award as this year’s established designer. Sources indicate that architecture project of the year was awarded to Daichi’s treetop sauna. The architecture project categories were also sponsored by Michelmersh and Sanderson.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by José Hevia.

Spanish studio Raúl Sánchez Architects turned a former washhouse into Casa de las Lavanderas, with a lightwell that is a “modern translation of the old wells” used by local laundry workers.

The home is located on Barcelona’s picturesque Calle Aiguafreda street, historically an area where washerwomen used wells to handwash their clients’ clothes.

Raúl Sánchez Architects, which won interiors project of the year at this year’s Dezeen Awards, turned one of the old laundry houses on the street into the two-storey Casa de las Lavanderas.

The house is now home to a couple and their newborn baby.

The lower level of the 80-square-metre building was partly underground and very dark, leading the studio to look for newly introduced solutions to add more light.

“Since the ground floor is semi-basement, the area furthest from Aiguafreda Street was darker, so to bring light into it, I incorporated this lightwell topped with a skylight,” studio founder Rául Sánchez told Dezeen.

The lightwell also functions as a “modern translation of the old wells” that used to provide water for the laundry workers.

Casa de las Lavanderas faces two streets – Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers – and has entrances on both sides, with the Calle Aiguafreda entrance sitting 1.5 metres lower than that on Calle Granollers.

From here, one flight of stairs leads down to the lower level and the Calle Aiguafreda entrance, and another up to the house’s upper level.

The 40-square-metre lower level houses an open-proposal living, dining and kitchen area, a bathroom and a small study.

This can be partitioned off from the living space using folding doors made from wood and rice paper, inspired by the clients’ time living in Japan.

In the kitchen, Sánchez remarked he added a mirror-clad island to “introduce a sense of fragility without disrupting the open feel of the space”.

The upper level, meanwhile, houses the home’s bedrooms and a bathroom. The two floors are connected by the Klein-blue lightwell, which has oculi on all four sides to help distribute the illumination from its skylight throughout the space.

Sánchez wanted to “bring that picturesque atmosphere of Aiguafreda Street into the house, making it part of its surroundings by reclaiming that well – now translated into a lightwell that also helps regulate the home’s temperature.”.

This was one of many tailor-made solutions to turn the former laundry house into a home.

“There were many challenges, both technical – access to the mezzanine level, the upcoming staircase, the structural reinforcements – and functional, like fitting the program into just 80 square metres,” Sánchez mentioned.

His studio also worked with materials that would complement the existing ones, using terracotta tiles on the ground floor to extend the traditional exterior clay paving and adding colored glazed tiles to the washbasins and bathroom walls.

“Ultimately, the goal is always to create a cohesive, overarching project that addresses all these challenges and offers something extra – something almost hard to put into words, but that translates into simply feeling good in the space,” Sánchez concluded.

Rául Sánchez Architects is currently working on the final phase of the project, the design of its orchard and garden, which will begin at the start of 2027.

The studio also recently designed a concrete home with a sunken courtyard in Cala Tamarit.

Architecture team: Nerea Moya, Marta Gámiz, FlaviaStructure consultant: Diagonal EstructurasEngineering consultant: Mares Engyniers.

Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people.
  • In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb.
  • Industry observers note that if you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas, tells SELF. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

Industry observers note that if you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller indicates, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

In a recent development, at the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.).

Recent findings suggest that by contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran claims. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

In a recent development, if you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication right about now. Pollen counts are rising, and antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.).

It has been revealed that the less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

In a recent development, whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller states to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

Industry observers note that if the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran states. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she claims.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller indicates. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

According to recent reports, if you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable. (Photo: Challenge Family).

Recent findings suggest that we know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves. Either it’s too cold outside or it’s too beautiful a day to pass up a bike ride. Or perhaps there’s a storm 100 miles away that might suddenly decide to blow right over the aquatics center. But the truth is, if your workout is interesting enough, you’ll have all the excuses you need to get yourself into the pool, not out of it.

It has been revealed that and we’re not just talking about adding in a random drill here and there. Gamifying your swim workout, whether through solo exercises or team activities, helps make a workout enticing enough that you’ll want to do it over and over again. Adding an element of play to your swim can make it more challenging, productive, and fun all at once.

Before we get into a handful of our favorite games and drills, we asked Sage Hopkins, head coach of Women’s Swimming & Diving at San José State University, for his tips on how to make swimming more enjoyable. With these tools in your arsenal, you might not skip your pool workouts anymore, but actually look forward to them instead.

It has been revealed that first, Hopkins stresses how crucial it is to hear laughter echoing across the pool deck. This might not be possible if you’re training alone, but if you have a training buddy who always keeps you smiling, make it a priority to meet with them more regularly. Hopkins also encourages using music to establish an upbeat atmosphere; that might look like playing a pump-up song on your way to the pool, or investing in a pair of swimming headphones to keep the tunes going lap after lap.

Once you know your purpose, Hopkins claims, it’s easier to figure out what kinds of activities will make swimming more meaningful and enjoyable. Those who enjoy the camaraderie aspect of swimming and triathlon will enjoy team games like sharks and minnows.

Industry observers note that even simple details like naming a set, Hopkins notes, can add a thrill to swimming. If there’s a test set you’re always dreading, give it a quirky or amusing name to make it seem less intimidating. You could use the most challenging triathlon you’ve ever lined up for as inspiration (The Wales One Hundreds, for instance, or the Norseman No Breathers).

Now, without further ado, let the games begin!

In a recent development, you don’t need any fancy clubs to play a round of swim golf — just enough glycogen in your head to add numbers. Hopkins suggests this drill for data-driven triathletes because it’s easy to keep track of your progression over time. Essentially, you add the number of strokes with the number of seconds that it takes you to complete a certain distance (such as 50 yards) to get a “score.” You’ll then repeat that distance several times within a single set, trying to keep your score as low as possible. This game helps improve your distance per stroke and ultimately conserve energy.

In a recent development, healthy suspense invites bursts of dopamine and curiosity into your workout, and it also means that there’s no one to blame but fate for back-to-back sprint sets. Make sure to write the following rules down on a whiteboard or protected piece of paper to reduce confusion.

Start by grabbing a set of waterproof playing cards, and assign a technique to each suit; for example, spades might call for kicking, hearts for drills, diamonds for swimming, and clubs for pulling. Next, assign a distance to groups of numbers (for instance, 2s and 3s might mean 50s, while 4s and 5s might mean 100s, and so on). Keep your jacks, queens, kings, and aces in a separate pile because they’ll dictate the number of repeats (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively).

It has been revealed that so, for example, pulling a 5 of clubs alongside a queen would require you to grab your pull buoy for 2×100. Pulling a 2 of hearts alongside an ace would mean a 5×50 drill.

In a recent development, another way to bring a measure of unpredictability to your workout is to roll a single die four times to determine your next set. The first roll determines your technique (5s could require kicking), the second your effort level (perhaps 4s always mean sprints), the third your distance (1s could mean 50s), and the fourth your number of reps (anywhere from 1 to 6).

If you were on a summer swim team as a kid, chances are high you played many games of sharks and minnows. The game starts out with one “shark” who tries to tag all the other “minnows” as they swim from one side of the pool to the other. Each swimmer who gets tagged turns into a shark for the next round. You can complicate this game by instituting an underwater safety zone.

According to recent reports, if you have an area of the pool to yourself, form teams, set up goals on opposite walls with pull buoys, grab a ball, and play water polo. This is an excellent way to make vertical kicking, sprinting, and treading water more exciting. It also facilitates team bonding.

Head to the deep end for this game to work on endurance as you tread water and practice vertical kicking. If the lifeguards allow it, you can play water volleyball over the flags with an inflatable beach ball. Your pool might even have a water volleyball net, and some versions float so that you can move them as required.

In a recent development, hopkins recommends “call it sets,” inspired by Bob Steele, to work on pacing and fine-tuning your internal clock. Essentially, you and your training partners will swim a set of 100s, and before each repeat, each one of you will predict the time you expect to hit. Whoever is closest to their estimates wins the set.

Chase sets are a fun way for training groups with seemingly disparate ability levels to unite, says Hopkins. Slower swimmers are allowed a head start, while faster swimmers are tasked with trying to catch them. Chase sets are ideally employed for speedwork, not drills.

In a recent development, casino night is extraordinarily fun for large teams and helps highlight everyone’s unique talents. First, two or three swimmers who are roughly equivalent in speed line up at the blocks. Then, the other teammates line up behind the swimmer they predict will win.

According to recent reports, from there, you’ll use cards or dice to determine the “event” that the swimmers will be competing in (see general rules above in the solo workouts). Whoever has picked the winning swimmer gets a rest break while the rest of the team completes a penalty swim (a 50 sprint, perhaps). If you have one seemingly unbeatable swimmer on the team, you can assign them a permanent handicap.

London Museum brings "back a bit of London's heritage" with Smithfield Market opening
